sections.title: A relation is just a bundle of connections & related topics

board_events.text: What is a RELATION?
A relation R on a set A is simply a chosen collection of connected pairs.
Picture an arrow between two students whenever 'sits in the same row as' is true.
It is nothing more than a subset of all possible ordered pairs $(a,b)$.
Two boring extremes
Three traits that judge a relation
Reflexive is the self-loop: does every element relate to itself?
Symmetric is the two-way street: if a links to b, does b link back to a?
Transitive is the chain: if a to b and b to c, is the shortcut a to c present?
Antisymmetric is different: $(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$ in $R$ force $a=b$. Not the opposite of symmetric.

segments.text: <curious>Let's begin with the simplest possible idea. Forget every formula for a minute. A relation is just a rule that decides which pairs of things are connected.
Picture every student in your batch. Draw an arrow from one to another whenever the rule sits in the same row as is true. That whole bundle of arrows is the relation.
We don't draw arrows forever, though. We just list the connected pairs as ordered pairs, a and b, and collect them into one set.
So a relation R on a set A is nothing grander than a chosen subset of A cross A, the set of every ordered pair you could possibly form.
That is the entire definition. Pick some pairs, leave the rest out, and the collection you kept is your relation.
Two extremes are worth naming first. If you connect nothing to anything, you get the empty, or void, relation.
If you connect everything to everything, you get the universal relation, all of A cross A.
And if every element connects only to itself, like the rule is the same person as, you get the identity relation, I sub A.
The interesting relations live between the extremes, and we judge them by three personality traits.
First, reflexive, the self-loop. Does every single element relate to itself? Is in the same class as passes, because you are obviously in the same class as yourself.
Formally, reflexive means the pair a comma a sits in R for every a in A. Miss even one self-loop, and the relation is no longer reflexive.
Second, symmetric, the two-way street. If a is connected to b, is b automatically connected back to a? Is a neighbour of is symmetric.
Formally, whenever a comma b is in R, the reverse pair b comma a must also be in R.
Third, transitive, the chain or shortcut. If a links to b and b links to c, must the shortcut a to c exist? Lives in the same city as is transitive.
Formally, if both a comma b and b comma c sit in R, then a comma c must sit in R too.
<excited>Watch out for one look-alike. Antisymmetric says if both a comma b and b comma a are present, then a equals b. It is a completely different idea, not the opposite of symmetric.
This diagram shows all three at once on a tiny set a, b, c: self-loops for reflexive, matched reverse arrows for symmetric, and the red shortcut arrow for transitive.
Now the star of the show. A relation that has all three traits at once, reflexive and symmetric and transitive together, earns a special name: an equivalence relation.
In symbols, equivalence equals reflexive and symmetric and transitive, all holding simultaneously. Any one missing, and it is not an equivalence relation.
Think of the railway network. Is directly connected by a train is symmetric but not transitive, since two direct routes need not join into one.
But change the rule to can reach by any sequence of trains, and suddenly it becomes reflexive, symmetric, and transitive all at once.
The superpower of an equivalence relation is sorting. The class of a, written square-bracket a, is the set of all x that relate to a.
<whisper>Here is the exam-critical fact: these distinct classes never overlap, and together they cover the whole set. They partition A into neat buckets.
Each bucket is one equivalence class, a group of mutually reachable, mutually related elements, completely separate from the others.
The diagram shows exactly this: three sealed buckets, fully connected inside, with no arrows crossing between them.
In this subtopic, counting formulas play the role that formulas play in physics. Let us derive the headline one and then list the rest.
A relation on A is a subset of A cross A. Now A cross A has n times n, that is n squared, ordered pairs inside it.
Each of those n squared pairs is independently either in R or out of R, two choices each, so the total number of relations is two raised to n squared.
That two-choices-per-pair logic is the whole engine. Reflexive relations just force the n self-pairs to be present.
With n self-pairs locked in, only n squared minus n pairs stay free, so reflexive relations number two raised to n squared minus n.
Symmetric relations pair up off-diagonal entries, leaving n times n plus one over two free choices, giving two raised to that exponent.
<whisper>And the prize one: the number of equivalence relations equals the n-th Bell number, because equivalence relations match one-to-one with partitions of the set.
Memorise the opening Bell numbers, one, two, five, fifteen, fifty two. They turn many JEE counting questions into instant answers.
Let us turn the traits into a fast routine you can run under exam pressure, then apply it to a real relation.
Step one, always test reflexive first. It is the cheapest check, and a single missing self-pair instantly kills reflexivity and equivalence, saving you the harder work.
For symmetric and transitive, do not verify everything. Just hunt for one counterexample, because a single broken case is enough to reject the property.
Take A equals one, two, three, four, with R holding the four self-pairs plus one comma two, two comma one, and three comma four.
Reflexive check. We need every a comma a. All four, one one, two two, three three, four four, are present, so R is reflexive.
Symmetric check. The pair three comma four sits in R, but its reverse four comma three does not. One missing reverse, and symmetry is dead.
Transitive check. Every chain we can form, like one two then two one giving one one, lands on a pair already inside R. So transitivity holds.
Verdict: R is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric, and therefore not an equivalence relation.
This example carries the single most popular trap in the whole subtopic, so slow down here.
Let A be one, two, three, and let R one be the empty relation, with no pairs at all inside it.
Here is the twist. The empty relation is vacuously symmetric and vacuously transitive, but it is not reflexive on a non-empty set.
Why? Symmetry and transitivity are if-then statements. With no pairs, the if part never triggers, so there is no counterexample, and the property holds for free.
Now a counting warm-up. On the three-element set, the number of relations is two raised to three squared, which is two to the nine, equals five hundred twelve.
Next, take R with all three self-pairs plus one comma two and two comma one. Test it: reflexive, symmetric, and transitive all pass.
So R is already an equivalence relation, and the number of pairs you must add is zero. The trap is helpfully adding two comma three and over-merging.
Finally, how many equivalence relations contain one comma two? Only the partition one-two alone with three, and the all-together partition. Exactly two.

segments.text: This is the model proof worth memorising, because congruence modulo n is the archetype of every equivalence relation you will meet.
Fix a positive integer n. Define a related to b to mean that a minus b is divisible by n, for integers a and b.
Reflexive first. For any integer a, the difference a minus a is zero, and zero is divisible by everything, including n.
In symbols, a minus a equals zero equals n times zero. So every integer trivially relates to itself, and reflexivity holds.
Symmetric next. Suppose a relates to b, so a minus b equals n times some integer k. Divisibility is not disturbed by a sign flip.
Then b minus a equals minus of a minus b, which is n times minus k, still a multiple of n. So b relates to a, and symmetry holds.
Transitive last. Suppose a minus b is n k one and b minus c is n k two. Add these two differences together.
The middle term b cancels, leaving a minus c equals n times k one plus k two, a multiple of n. So a relates to c, and transitivity holds.
All three hold, so R is an equivalence relation, and its classes are the residues zero through n minus one, partitioning the integers into exactly n buckets.
Now a JEE Advanced pairing that contrasts a fake equivalence with a real one, on the whole real line.
Define a R one b as the absolute value of a minus b being at most one, and a R two b as a minus b being an integer.
For R one, reflexive is fine since the distance from a point to itself is zero, and symmetric is fine since distance ignores order. But transitivity is the problem.
Take a equals zero, b equals one, c equals two. Zero to one has distance one, one to two has distance one, yet zero to two has distance two, which exceeds one.
That counterexample kills transitivity. The moral is worth keeping: closeness relations almost always break transitivity, because small gaps quietly accumulate.
R two is a different animal. Two reals relate exactly when their difference is a whole number, which means they share the same fractional part. This is a genuine equivalence.

Each class is a copy of the integers shifted by x, that is all numbers x plus k for integer k. For example, the class of zero point three contains minus zero point seven, zero point three, one point three, and so on.
So the classes are labelled by the fractional part, which always lives in the interval from zero up to but not including one, and every fractional value gives a different class.
The diagram makes it visible: three colour-coded class systems, each an evenly spaced set of points seeded by its own fractional part, never colliding.
Let us close the subtopic with the traps that quietly drain marks, then the speed habits that save time.
Trap one, the biggest board-exam slip. Finding a few self-pairs and stopping is not reflexivity. You need a comma a for every single element of A.
Trap two, the empty relation. It is symmetric and transitive vacuously, but never reflexive on a non-empty set. Do not write empty, so no properties.
Trap three, symmetric and antisymmetric are not opposites. The identity relation is both. Many relations are neither. Not symmetric never implies antisymmetric.
Trap four, every trait is relative to the underlying set A. The same list of pairs can be reflexive on one set and fail on a larger one, so always state the set.
Now the speed habits that make classification fast under time pressure.
Always test reflexive first, since one missing self-pair kills equivalence immediately. For symmetric and transitive, hunt a single counterexample rather than checking everything.
And memorise the three counting exponents: relations use n squared, reflexive uses n squared minus n, symmetric uses n times n plus one over two.
Now we move from relations to functions. A function is a machine with one strict rule: feed it one input, and it returns exactly one output.
A vending machine is the perfect picture. Press the button for cold coffee and you get exactly one cold coffee. Never nothing, never two different drinks at once.
That wiring from inputs to outputs is the function f from A to B, where A is the domain of valid buttons and B is the codomain of every slot the machine could reach.
<curious>The types of functions are just answers to two simple questions. Here is question one: do different buttons ever give the same drink?
If no two different inputs ever share an output, the function is one-one, also called injective. Think of Aadhaar numbers, where every citizen gets a distinct number.
Formally, injective means that whenever f of x one equals f of x two, the inputs x one and x two must actually be equal.
The opposite is many-one, where two or more inputs collapse to the same output. Whenever you spot an even power or a plus-minus symmetry, suspect many-one. Both plus two and minus two map to four.
The diagram contrasts a clean one-one mapping, where distinct inputs hit distinct outputs, with a many-one mapping, where two inputs crash into a single output.
Here is question two about the wiring: does every slot in the codomain actually get used?
If every element of the codomain has at least one input pointing to it, the function is onto, also called surjective. Picture a full bus with every seat occupied.
Formally, surjective means for every y in B there exists some x in A with f of x equal to y, which is the same as saying the range equals the whole codomain B.
The opposite is into, where some codomain elements are never reached, leaving empty seats behind.
The squaring machine from the reals to the reals is a clean example of into, because no negative number is ever an output, so the entire negative half of the codomain sits empty.
<excited>Now put both answers together. A function that is one-one and onto is bijective, a flawless pairing where every input has a private output and every output is claimed.
Bijective equals one-one and onto, and crucially, it equals invertible. Bijections are exactly the functions you can run backwards, which we will exploit in composition and inverses.
One graphical shortcut: sweep a horizontal line across the graph. If it ever cuts the curve twice, two inputs share an output, so it fails one-one. A parabola fails; a straight line passes.
Let us pin down the definitions cleanly and collect the structural facts that turn many questions into one-liners.
The two negations: many-one means some pair of distinct inputs shares an output, and into means the range is a strict subset of the codomain, not all of it.
A few special maps repay memory. The identity map is always bijective. A constant map is many-one, and it is into whenever the codomain has more than one element.
A powerful fact for real polynomials from the reals to the reals: odd degree forces onto, while even degree forces into and can never be onto.
Another shortcut: a strictly monotonic function, always increasing or always decreasing, is automatically one-one, because a curve that never turns back can never revisit an output.
<whisper>Now the trap that catches most students. The type of a function depends entirely on the declared domain and codomain, not on the formula alone.

Watch x squared change character. From the reals to the reals it is into. From the reals to zero-to-infinity it becomes onto. From zero-to-infinity to itself it is fully bijective. Same formula, three answers.
So the question is this function onto is incomplete until the codomain B is fixed. Always read the sets before you classify.

board_events.text: Four counts, four feasibility gates
Each of the n inputs independently picks one of m images.
Watch base versus exponent: it is $m^n$, not $n^m$.
Feasibility: no one-one map when the domain is bigger, no onto when the codomain is bigger.
The two testing routines
One-one: assume f of x1 equals f of x2 and try to force x1 equals x2.
Onto: solve y equals f of x for x, and ask if a valid x exists for every y.
One-one: 2x1 minus 7 equals 2x2 minus 7 collapses straight to x1 equals x2.
Onto: solve for x and check it is real for every real y.
Count by type, mind the direction
Functions from X to Y: each of four inputs picks one of five images.
One-one from X to Y is feasible since five is at least four.
Onto from Y to X needs inclusion-exclusion, feasible since five is at least four.
Classify, then restrict
Onto: an odd-degree polynomial sweeps from minus infinity to plus infinity, hitting every value.
One-one fails: the derivative changes sign, so the curve turns back.
$f(0)=0$ and $f(\sqrt{3})=0$: two inputs share the output $0$, so many-one.
Restrict to x at least one, where the derivative stays non-negative, and adjust the codomain.

Declaring 'onto' without stating the codomain: compare the range with $B$, not with $\mathbb{R}$ by reflex.

Into is a valid function type, not a broken function; it simply means not onto.

For differentiable maps, check monotonicity first: a one-sign derivative means one-one, no algebra.
Composition: functions in series
A two-stage water system: an RO purifier feeds a chiller, giving cold clean water.
Run f first, then feed its output into g.
Innermost first: in $g \circ f$, even though $g$ is on the left, $f$ touches $x$ first.

segments.text: These counting formulas are the formulas of this subtopic, and every one carries a feasibility gate you must respect.
Start with all functions from A to B. Each of the n inputs independently picks one of m possible images, so the total is m raised to the power n.
That multiplication logic is the base. Read the count as m to the n, and be careful never to swap base and exponent.
For injective, or one-one, functions, the count is m permute n, that is m factorial over m minus n factorial. This is only feasible when m is at least n.
For bijective functions the two sets must have equal size, m equals n, and the count is simply n factorial, the number of perfect pairings.
For surjective, or onto, functions we need inclusion-exclusion: the alternating sum over k of minus one to the k, times m choose k, times m minus k to the n. Feasible only when n is at least m.
A constant reminder in the exam: it is m to the n, not n to the m. Swapping base and exponent is a classic slip that changes the answer completely.
And keep the feasibility gates handy. There is no one-one map when the domain is bigger than the codomain, and no onto map when the codomain is bigger than the domain.
Let us convert the two questions into concrete testing routines, then prove a linear function is a bijection.
To test one-one algebraically, assume f of x one equals f of x two, and try to force x one equals x two. If you can, it is one-one.
To test onto, solve y equals f of x for x in terms of y, then ask whether a valid x in the domain exists for every y in the codomain.
Take f from the reals to the reals given by f of x equals two x minus seven, the classic board-exam bijection.
One-one test. Set two x one minus seven equal to two x two minus seven. The minus seven cancels, the two divides out, and you are left with x one equals x two.
Written out, two x one minus seven equals two x two minus seven forces x one equals x two directly. So the function is one-one.
Onto test. Take any real y and solve y equals two x minus seven for x, which gives x equals y plus seven over two.
That x is a real number for every real y, and it maps back to y, so every y has a preimage. The function is onto, and therefore bijective.
Now a three-part counting example that exercises all three formulas and, crucially, the direction of the map.
Let X have four elements and Y have five elements. We will count plain functions, one-one functions, and onto functions in turn.
Part a, functions from X to Y. Each of the four inputs independently picks one of five images, using the m-to-the-n rule.
That gives five raised to the four, which equals six hundred twenty five.
Part b, one-one functions from X to Y. This is feasible because the codomain size five is at least the domain size four.
The count is five permute four, that is five factorial over one factorial, which equals one hundred twenty.
Part c reverses direction: onto functions from Y to X, feasible because five is at least four. Onto counting needs inclusion-exclusion to subtract maps that miss a target.
The alternating sum is four to the five, minus four choose one times three to the five, plus four choose two times two to the five, minus four choose three, and that works out to two hundred forty.
This JEE Advanced example shows how to diagnose a function and then surgically restrict it into a bijection.
Take f from the reals to the reals given by f of x equals x cubed minus three x, and classify it before repairing it.
Onto first. This is an odd-degree polynomial, continuous, sweeping from minus infinity up to plus infinity, so by the intermediate value theorem it attains every real value. It is onto.
One-one next, and here it fails. The derivative changes sign, which means the curve rises, turns, and falls, so it must revisit some outputs.
The derivative is three x squared minus three, which factors as three times x minus one times x plus one, zero at plus and minus one, and it changes sign there.
Concretely, f of zero is zero and f of root three is also zero. Two different inputs share the output zero, so the function is many-one on the reals.
To repair it, restrict the domain to x at least one. On that branch the derivative stays non-negative, so the function is strictly increasing and hence one-one.
Its image on that branch starts at f of one, which is one minus three equals minus two, so choosing the codomain minus two to infinity makes it onto too.
The final restricted map, from one-to-infinity to minus-two-to-infinity, is bijective, as the shaded increasing branch in the graph shows.
Let us close functions with the classification traps, then the reflexes that make you fast.
Trap one, declaring onto without stating the codomain. Onto is meaningless until B is fixed, so compare the range with the given B, not with the reals out of habit.
Trap two, forgetting that even powers, absolute value, and trig functions are many-one. The plus-minus symmetry or periodicity silently kills injectivity, so check it before any algebra.
Trap three, confusing into with not a function. Into is a perfectly valid function type. It simply means not onto, so do not reject the map.
Trap four, counting blunders. Use m permute n for one-one, never m to the n, and always respect the feasibility gates on domain and codomain sizes.
Now the speed reflexes that save real time in the exam.
For differentiable functions, check monotonicity first. If the derivative keeps one sign throughout, the function is one-one and you are done, with no algebra at all.
And keep the sanity checks ready: odd degree means onto, even degree means into, and if the domain is larger than the codomain, one-one is simply impossible.
<curious>Now we chain functions together. Picture a two-stage water system at home: first an RO purifier, then a chiller.
Pour in tap water, the purifier cleans it, and its output immediately feeds the chiller, which cools it. Tap water in, cold clean water out.
That is exactly composition. The composite g after f, written g ring f, is defined as g of f of x.
In words, run f first, then feed its output straight into g. The order of operations is the whole story here.
Build one habit above all: the innermost function acts first. In g ring f, even though g sits on the left, it is f that touches x first.
Composition is a relay race, and swapping who runs first usually changes the race. So in general g ring f is not equal to f ring g. It is not commutative.
It is, however, associative. Chaining three machines gives the same result no matter how you group them, so h ring, bracket g ring f, equals bracket h ring g, ring f.
The diagram shows the relay clearly: x enters f, f hands its output to g, and the final result comes out, with f always acting first.

For injective, or one-one, functions, the count is m permute n, that is m factorial over m minus n factorial. This is only feasible when m is at least n.
For bijective functions the two sets must have equal size, m equals n, and the count is simply n factorial, the number of perfect pairings.
For surjective, or onto, functions we need inclusion-exclusion: the alternating sum over k of minus one to the k, times m choose k, times m minus k to the n. Feasible only when n is at least m.
A constant reminder in the exam: it is m to the n, not n to the m. Swapping base and exponent is a classic slip that changes the answer completely.
And keep the feasibility gates handy. There is no one-one map when the domain is bigger than the codomain, and no onto map when the codomain is bigger than the domain.
Let us convert the two questions into concrete testing routines, then prove a linear function is a bijection.
To test one-one algebraically, assume f of x one equals f of x two, and try to force x one equals x two. If you can, it is one-one.
To test onto, solve y equals f of x for x in terms of y, then ask whether a valid x in the domain exists for every y in the codomain.
Take f from the reals to the reals given by f of x equals two x minus seven, the classic board-exam bijection.
One-one test. Set two x one minus seven equal to two x two minus seven. The minus seven cancels, the two divides out, and you are left with x one equals x two.
Written out, two x one minus seven equals two x two minus seven forces x one equals x two directly. So the function is one-one.
Onto test. Take any real y and solve y equals two x minus seven for x, which gives x equals y plus seven over two.
That x is a real number for every real y, and it maps back to y, so every y has a preimage. The function is onto, and therefore bijective.
Now a three-part counting example that exercises all three formulas and, crucially, the direction of the map.
Let X have four elements and Y have five elements. We will count plain functions, one-one functions, and onto functions in turn.
Part a, functions from X to Y. Each of the four inputs independently picks one of five images, using the m-to-the-n rule.
That gives five raised to the four, which equals six hundred twenty five.
Part b, one-one functions from X to Y. This is feasible because the codomain size five is at least the domain size four.
The count is five permute four, that is five factorial over one factorial, which equals one hundred twenty.
Part c reverses direction: onto functions from Y to X, feasible because five is at least four. Onto counting needs inclusion-exclusion to subtract maps that miss a target.
The alternating sum is four to the five, minus four choose one times three to the five, plus four choose two times two to the five, minus four choose three, and that works out to two hundred forty.
This JEE Advanced example shows how to diagnose a function and then surgically restrict it into a bijection.
Take f from the reals to the reals given by f of x equals x cubed minus three x, and classify it before repairing it.
Onto first. This is an odd-degree polynomial, continuous, sweeping from minus infinity up to plus infinity, so by the intermediate value theorem it attains every real value. It is onto.
One-one next, and here it fails. The derivative changes sign, which means the curve rises, turns, and falls, so it must revisit some outputs.
The derivative is three x squared minus three, which factors as three times x minus one times x plus one, zero at plus and minus one, and it changes sign there.
Concretely, f of zero is zero and f of root three is also zero. Two different inputs share the output zero, so the function is many-one on the reals.
To repair it, restrict the domain to x at least one. On that branch the derivative stays non-negative, so the function is strictly increasing and hence one-one.
Its image on that branch starts at f of one, which is one minus three equals minus two, so choosing the codomain minus two to infinity makes it onto too.
The final restricted map, from one-to-infinity to minus-two-to-infinity, is bijective, as the shaded increasing branch in the graph shows.
Let us close functions with the classification traps, then the reflexes that make you fast.
Trap one, declaring onto without stating the codomain. Onto is meaningless until B is fixed, so compare the range with the given B, not with the reals out of habit.
Trap two, forgetting that even powers, absolute value, and trig functions are many-one. The plus-minus symmetry or periodicity silently kills injectivity, so check it before any algebra.
Trap three, confusing into with not a function. Into is a perfectly valid function type. It simply means not onto, so do not reject the map.
Trap four, counting blunders. Use m permute n for one-one, never m to the n, and always respect the feasibility gates on domain and codomain sizes.
Now the speed reflexes that save real time in the exam.
For differentiable functions, check monotonicity first. If the derivative keeps one sign throughout, the function is one-one and you are done, with no algebra at all.
And keep the sanity checks ready: odd degree means onto, even degree means into, and if the domain is larger than the codomain, one-one is simply impossible.
<curious>Now we chain functions together. Picture a two-stage water system at home: first an RO purifier, then a chiller.
Pour in tap water, the purifier cleans it, and its output immediately feeds the chiller, which cools it. Tap water in, cold clean water out.
That is exactly composition. The composite g after f, written g ring f, is defined as g of f of x.
In words, run f first, then feed its output straight into g. The order of operations is the whole story here.
Build one habit above all: the innermost function acts first. In g ring f, even though g sits on the left, it is f that touches x first.
Composition is a relay race, and swapping who runs first usually changes the race. So in general g ring f is not equal to f ring g. It is not commutative.
It is, however, associative. Chaining three machines gives the same result no matter how you group them, so h ring, bracket g ring f, equals bracket h ring g, ring f.
The diagram shows the relay clearly: x enters f, f hands its output to g, and the final result comes out, with f always acting first.

board_events.text: Inverse: the undo button
Pressing control Z reverses the last action, landing you exactly where you started.

board_events.latex: f^{-1} \circ f = I \quad \text{and} \quad f \circ f^{-1} = I

board_events.text: The inverse is defined as the thing that composes with f to give 'do nothing'.
Not every function has an inverse: $f$ must be bijective (one-one and onto).
If f were many-one, f inverse of a shared output could not decide which input to return.

board_events.text: Inheritance: if f and g are both injective, so is g ring f; likewise surjective and bijective.

board_events.text: The superscript $-1$ means inverse function, never the reciprocal $\tfrac{1}{f(x)}$.
Substitute, then simplify
Rule: put the whole formula of the inner function into every input slot of the outer, then simplify.
Test x equal to two: f ring g gives seven, g ring f gives forty seven.
So $f \circ g \ne g \circ f$ — composition is genuinely not commutative.
Always confirm the handoff: the inner range must lie inside the outer domain.
Swap-and-solve, and involutions
Steps: check bijectivity, write y equals f of x, solve for x, then swap x and y.
Trap: $f^{-1}(x) \ne \dfrac{1}{7 - 3x}$ — the reciprocal is not the inverse.
A self-inverse, or involution, returns x when you apply it twice.
To spot a self-inverse fast, compose the function with itself and look for x.
Inverse of a rational map
Set y equal to the expression and clear the fraction.
Sanity check: $\mathrm{Dom}(f^{-1}) = \mathrm{Range}(f)$ and $\mathrm{Range}(f^{-1}) = \mathrm{Dom}(f)$.
When the domain-range swap holds, your inverse is confirmed correct.
Socks and shoes, confirmed
Now the second route: invert each piece, then reverse the order.
Both routes match: $(g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$ — undo the last step first.

segments.text: Now meet the undo button. Picture pressing control Z: whatever the last action did, undo reverses it perfectly, landing you exactly where you started.
An inverse function f inverse is the control Z of f. If f sends a to b, then f inverse sends b straight back to a.
Formally, f inverse composed with f is the identity, and f composed with f inverse is also the identity, where identity is the do-nothing function.
Composition and inverse meet right here: the inverse is defined as the thing that composes with f to give do nothing.
But here is the catch. Not every function has an inverse. For the undo to work, f must be bijective, that is one-one and onto.
Why bijective? If f were many-one, say both two and minus two map to four, then f inverse of four could not decide whether to return two or minus two. The undo is ambiguous.
And if f were not onto, some target would have no input to return to. So f is invertible exactly when f is bijective, the bridge straight from the previous subtopic.
Geometrically, the inverse is the mirror image of f across the line y equals x, as this reflection diagram shows.
Let us gather the properties you will lean on in every problem, first for composition, then for inverse.
Composition sends A to C through B, defined by g of f of x, and it only makes sense when the range of the inner f lies inside the domain of the outer g.
The identity is neutral: composing f with the identity on either side just gives f back, so f ring identity equals f equals identity ring f.
Composition also inherits good behaviour. If f and g are both injective, so is g ring f, and the same holds for surjective and for bijective.
For the inverse: f inverse composed with f is the identity on A, and f composed with f inverse is the identity on B, and it exists exactly when f is bijective.
Two more: undoing an inverse gives back the original, so f inverse inverse equals f, and the domain of f inverse is the range of f.
The star property, order reversal: the inverse of g ring f equals f inverse ring g inverse. You undo the last-applied function first.
And the constant warning: the superscript minus one means the inverse function, never the reciprocal one over f of x. Keep those two apart.
Let us make composition concrete by computing both orders and seeing them disagree.
The rule is mechanical: take the whole formula of the inner function and drop it into every input slot of the outer one, then simplify.
Take f of x equals three x plus one and g of x equals x squared minus two, both on the reals.
For f ring g, feed g into f. Wherever f says input, write x squared minus two. So three times x squared minus two, plus one, giving three x squared minus five.
For g ring f, feed f into g. Square three x plus one and subtract two, which expands to nine x squared plus six x minus one.
Test at x equal to two. f ring g gives seven, while g ring f gives forty seven. Very different numbers from the same two functions.
So f ring g is not equal to g ring f. Composition is genuinely not commutative, and order is never optional.
One habit before you finish: always confirm the handoff, meaning the range of the inner function must lie inside the domain of the outer function.
Here is the standard recipe for an inverse, plus a neat special case you should recognise on sight.
The steps: first check the function is bijective, then write y equals f of x, solve for x in terms of y, and finally swap x and y to name f inverse.

Take f of x equals seven minus three x. It multiplies by minus three, then adds seven. Undo in reverse: subtract seven, then divide by minus three, giving f inverse of x equals seven minus x over three.
Guard against the classic trap. f inverse of x is not one over seven minus three x. The reciprocal is a completely different object from the inverse.
Now a special case. A self-inverse, also called an involution, is a function that returns x when you apply it twice.
Take p of x equals one over x. Applying it twice, p of p of x, gives one over one over x, which is just x. So p is its own inverse.
Contrast q of x equals two x. Applying it twice gives four x, which is not x, so q is not a self-inverse.
The fast test for a self-inverse is exactly this: compose the function with itself and check whether it collapses back to x.
Now invert a rational function, the kind that appears constantly in JEE Main. The method is swap and solve, handled carefully.
Take f from the reals without three to the reals without two, given by two x minus one over x minus three. Between those sets it is one-one and onto, so the inverse exists.
Set y equal to two x minus one over x minus three, then clear the fraction by multiplying across.
That gives y times x minus three equals two x minus one. Gather the x terms: x times y minus two equals three y minus one.
Solve for x, giving x equals three y minus one over y minus two.
Now swap y and x to name the inverse: f inverse of x equals three x minus one over x minus two, with domain the reals without two.
Do the sanity check. The domain of f inverse is the reals without two, which is exactly the range of f, and the range of f inverse is the reals without three, exactly the domain of f.
That domain-range swap holding is your built-in confirmation that the inverse is correct.
This example proves the order-reversal law by computing the same inverse two independent ways and watching them agree.
Take f of x equals x cubed plus two and g of x equals two x minus one, both on the reals.
Way one, direct. Build the composite g ring f: substitute f into g to get two times x cubed plus two, minus one, which is two x cubed plus three.
Invert that composite. Set y equals two x cubed plus three, solve, and you get the inverse equals the cube root of x minus three over two.
Way two uses the law. Invert each piece separately, then reverse the order of composition.
The inverses are f inverse of x equals the cube root of x minus two, and g inverse of x equals x plus one over two.
Now compose f inverse after g inverse. Feed x plus one over two into f inverse and simplify, and it collapses to the cube root of x minus three over two.
Both routes give exactly the same answer, confirming that the inverse of g ring f equals f inverse ring g inverse. Undo the last-applied step first.
The diagram captures it: doing f then g goes left to right, and undoing runs backward, g inverse first, then f inverse, like taking off shoes before socks.

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for composition and inverse & related topics

board_events.text: Where these problems go wrong
Composition is not commutative: $f \circ g$ and $g \circ f$ almost always differ; read innermost-first.
The reciprocal trap: $f^{-1}(x)$ is the inverse function, never $\tfrac{1}{f(x)}$.
No inverse exists unless f is bijective; if it is not, restrict the domain first.
Inverting a composite reverses the order: (g ring f) inverse equals f inverse ring g inverse.
Speed pro-tips
To evaluate f inverse at c without the whole inverse, just solve f of x equals c for x.
Verify any claimed inverse fast: if f of f inverse of x collapses to x, you are done.
Always state the domain of $f^{-1}$: it equals the range of $f$.
Domain: which inputs are allowed?
The domain is the list of ingredients the machine will accept without jamming.
Jam 1 — division by zero: any denominator equal to $0$ is forbidden.
Jam 2 — even root of a negative: the content under a square root must be at least zero.
Jam 3 — log of a non-positive number: a log argument must be strictly greater than zero.
Find every place these jams could occur, write each condition, and intersect them all.
Simultaneously means intersection, never union.
Range: which outputs can appear?
Range is harder than domain; you usually cannot just read it off.
The reliable trick: set y equal to f of x, solve for x, then ask which y give a legal x.

board_events.text: Those y-values, for which a real in-domain x exists, form the range.
The range depends on the domain: shrink the domain and the range can shrink too.
Range is not the codomain: '$f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$' does not mean every real is hit.

board_events.latex: \mathrm{Range}(f) \subseteq B, \ \text{with equality only when } f \text{ is onto}

board_events.text: Domain constraints at a glance
Standard ranges worth memorising
For a rational a x plus b over c x plus d, the range is all reals except a over c.
For a quadratic over a quadratic, cross-multiply and force the discriminant to be non-negative.
Root-plus-fraction, and a log
The root needs x minus three at least zero; the denominator needs x not equal to five.
Only one constraint: the log argument must be strictly positive, so x squared exceeds four.
Using $\ge 0$ here is the root rule; a log needs $> 0$, so $x = \pm 2$ is excluded.

Trap one, treating composition as commutative. f ring g and g ring f are almost always different, so respect the order and read innermost-first: in g ring f, f touches x first.
Trap two, the reciprocal trap. f inverse of x is the inverse function, never one over f of x. The same superscript means two different things on functions versus numbers.
Trap three, inverting a non-bijective function. No inverse exists unless f is one-one and onto. If it is not, you must restrict the domain or codomain first.
Trap four, keeping the same order when inverting a composite. The inverse of g ring f is f inverse ring g inverse, with the order reversed, socks and shoes.
Now the speed reflexes that make these problems quick.
To evaluate f inverse at a single value c, do not build the whole inverse. Just solve f of x equals c for x, and that one value is f inverse of c.
And to verify any claimed inverse in seconds, check that f of f inverse of x collapses to x. If it does, you are done.
One more habit: always state the domain of f inverse, because it equals the range of f, and examiners look for it.
<curious>Every function is a machine, and the domain answers one question: which inputs is it allowed to accept?
Think of a kitchen. The domain is the list of ingredients the recipe will accept. Hand it something it cannot process, and the machine jams.
There are exactly three jams to watch for. Jam one is division by zero: any denominator that becomes zero is forbidden, because the machine explodes there.
Jam two is an even root of a negative. The square root, or any even root, of a negative number is not real, so whatever sits under it must be at least zero.
Jam three is the logarithm of a non-positive number. A log only accepts strictly positive inputs, so the argument of any log must be greater than zero.
The routine is simple. Find every place these three jams could occur, write down the condition that avoids each one, and then intersect all the conditions.
That intersection is the domain, the set of x for which every constraint holds at the same time.
Say it aloud so it sticks: simultaneously means intersection, never union. Constraints meet, they do not merely mingle.
The range is the harder twin of the domain. Domain asks what may go in; range asks what can possibly come out.
And you usually cannot just read the range off the formula, so we need a reliable method rather than guessing.
The trick is to turn the machine inside out. Set y equal to f of x, solve for x in terms of y, and then ask for which values of y a legal x actually exists.
In symbols, y equals f of x, then x becomes some expression in y, and you keep only the y that produce a valid x.
Those y-values, the ones for which a real in-domain x exists, are exactly the range. You are asking the machine to run backwards and seeing which outputs have a source.
Two cautions. First, the range depends on the domain. Shrink the domain, and the range can shrink with it.
Second, the range is not automatically the codomain. Writing f from the reals to the reals only promises outputs land in the reals, not that every real is hit.
So the range is a subset of the codomain B, and they are equal only when the function is onto.
Here is the working catalogue: the domain constraints on one side, and the range shortcuts on the other.
For domains, a rational needs its denominator non-zero, and an even root needs its content at least zero.
Two sharper cases. A root sitting in a denominator needs its content strictly greater than zero, and a log needs its argument strictly greater than zero.
Now the standard ranges, worth committing to memory so you never re-derive them.
x squared and absolute value give zero to infinity, e to the x gives strictly positive reals, natural log gives all reals, and sine and cosine give minus one to one.
A powerful shortcut. For a rational, a x plus b over c x plus d, the range is all the reals except a single value.
That excluded value is a over c, the horizontal asymptote that the function approaches but never actually reaches.
And for a quadratic divided by a quadratic, do not guess. Cross-multiply into a quadratic in x and force its discriminant to be non-negative.
Let us apply the constraint catalogue to two problems, a sum with a root and a fraction, and a logarithm.
Take f of x equals the square root of x minus three plus one over x minus five, which mixes two different jams.
The root demands x minus three is at least zero, so x is at least three. The denominator demands x minus five is non-zero, so x is not five. Now intersect.
Intersecting, the domain is three up to five, including three but excluding five, together with everything beyond five. Written as three to five, union five to infinity.
Now the log example: g of x equals log of x squared minus four, which has just one constraint.
The log argument must be strictly positive, so x squared minus four is greater than zero, meaning x squared exceeds four, that is the absolute value of x is greater than two.
So the domain of g is everything below minus two, together with everything above two.

Watch the trap here. Writing greater than or equal to zero would be the root rule, but a log needs strictly greater than zero, so x equal to plus or minus two, where the log would be log of zero, is excluded.
The number line makes the first answer vivid: a solid stretch from three, an open hole at five, and an arrow continuing to infinity.
This example shows the y-method in its purest form: turn the range question into a discriminant condition.
Take f of x equals x over one plus x squared, defined for all real x.
First the domain. Since one plus x squared is always at least one, the denominator never vanishes, so the domain is all of the reals.
Now set y equal to x over one plus x squared and clear the fraction. Rearranging gives y x squared minus x plus y equals zero, a quadratic in x.
Here is the key idea. For a real input x to exist for a given y, this quadratic must have a non-negative discriminant.
The discriminant is minus one squared minus four times y times y, which must be at least zero, giving one minus four y squared is at least zero.
Solving, y squared is at most one quarter, so y lies between minus one half and one half. That closed interval is the range.
The graph shows exactly this trapping: the curve peaks at one half, bottoms at minus one half, and never escapes the band between them.

board_events.text: Range of a quadratic over a quadratic
The denominator is a shifted square plus three quarters, always positive, so the domain is all reals.
Force the discriminant to be non-negative so a real x exists.
Check the degenerate $y = 1$: it gives $x = 0$, valid, and $1$ already lies in the range.
A layered square-root-of-a-log
Constraint one: the inner log argument must be positive.
Constraint two: the square-root content must be non-negative, so the log is at least zero.
Base $\tfrac{1}{2} < 1$, so $\log_{1/2}(t) \ge 0$ means $t \le 1$: the inequality flips.
Where domain and range slip
Root rule versus log rule: under a root $\ge 0$, inside a log strictly $> 0$.
Multiple constraints must all hold together: always intersect, never union.
For a log base below one, the inequality flips: $\log_{1/2}(t) \ge 0 \iff 0 < t \le 1$.
The codomain is not the range: compute the actual outputs, do not assume all of the reals.
Speed pro-tips
For sin or cos builds, push the bound minus one to one through the operations rather than inverting.
A toolkit of named functions
Modulus, the absolute value, strips the sign and reports distance from zero; its graph is a V.
Signum keeps only the sign, outputting just minus one, zero, or plus one.
Greatest integer, the floor, rounds down to the nearest integer, even for negatives.
$[-2.3] = -3$, not $-2$: the floor always rounds down, past zero.
Fractional part keeps what the floor leaves, always in zero to one, giving a sawtooth.
Exponential is always positive; logarithm is its mirror, defined only for positive inputs.

segments.text: Now the full discriminant method on a quadratic over a quadratic, the exact template JEE loves to test.
Take f of x equals x squared minus x plus one, all over x squared plus x plus one.
First note the denominator can be written as x plus one half squared, plus three quarters, which is always positive, so the domain is all of the reals.
Set y equal to the whole fraction and cross-multiply. Collecting terms gives y minus one times x squared, plus y plus one times x, plus y minus one, equals zero.
This is a quadratic in x, so for a real x to exist for a given y, force its discriminant to be non-negative.
The discriminant condition is y plus one squared minus four times y minus one squared is at least zero, which factors neatly into three minus y times three y minus one is at least zero.
That product is non-negative for y between one third and three, so the range is the closed interval one third to three.
Finally check the degenerate case y equal to one, where the quadratic becomes linear. It gives x equal to zero, a valid input, and one already lies inside the range, so nothing changes.
This JEE Advanced problem layers a logarithm inside a square root, and the whole difficulty is one inequality flip.
Take f of x equals the square root of log base one half of the fraction x minus two over x plus one.
Constraint one comes from the inner log: its argument must be positive.
The fraction x minus two over x plus one is positive when x is below minus one or above two. Hold that set.
Constraint two comes from the square root: its content must be non-negative, which means the log itself must be at least zero.
<whisper>Here is the exam-deciding subtlety. The base is one half, which is below one, so log base one half of t being at least zero means t is at most one. The inequality flips direction.
So the fraction is at most one, which rearranges to minus three over x plus one is at most zero, and that holds when x is greater than minus one.
Now intersect the two constraints. The first gave x below minus one or above two; the second gave x above minus one; together they leave only x above two, so the domain is two to infinity.
Let us close domain and range with the traps that drain marks, then the shortcuts that save time.
Trap one, confusing the root rule with the log rule. Under a root the content is at least zero, but inside a log it is strictly greater than zero. Mixing them adds or drops boundary points.
Trap two, union instead of intersection. When several constraints apply, they must all hold together, so you always intersect, never union.
Trap three, forgetting the flip for a log base below one. Log base one half of t being at least zero means t is between zero and one, with the direction reversed.
Trap four, calling the codomain the range. f from the reals to the reals does not mean the range is all the reals, so always compute the actual outputs.
Now the shortcuts that make these instant.
For a rational a x plus b over c x plus d, the range is immediately all reals except a over c, with no algebra needed.
And for anything built from sine or cosine, push the known bound minus one to one through the operations, rather than inverting the whole function.
<curious>Before analysing functions, you need a toolkit of named machines you recognise instantly, the way a mechanic knows every tool by its shape.
The modulus, or absolute value, strips the sign and reports distance from zero, so it is never negative. Its graph is a V sitting on the origin.
Signum is the opposite idea. It throws away the size and keeps only the sign, outputting just minus one, zero, or plus one, giving two flat shelves.
The greatest integer, or floor, rounds down to the nearest integer, producing a staircase. Crucially, it rounds down even for negatives.
So floor of minus two point three is minus three, not minus two. The floor always rounds down, moving further from zero, and this single fact costs the most marks.
The fractional part keeps whatever the floor leaves behind, always landing in zero up to but not including one, which produces a repeating sawtooth.
Finally, the exponential is explosive controlled growth, always positive, never touching the x-axis, while the logarithm is the exponential run backwards, defined only for positive inputs.
The atlas shows all six shapes together, and memorising them is like memorising multiplication tables: it makes everything downstream automatic.
A complicated graph is usually just a base shape relocated, so learn to read graphs by transformation.
Start from a base graph and apply, in order, horizontal shifts, vertical shifts, stretches, and reflections. Each operation moves the picture in a predictable, decoupled way.
For example, f of x minus h plus k shifts the base graph right by h and up by k. Replace x by x minus h to slide right, then add k to lift up.
Now a distinction JEE tests again and again: the two modulus transformations, which look similar but do opposite things.
First, y equals the modulus of f of x. Take the graph of f and flip everything below the x-axis upward, because negative outputs become their positive mirror.
Second, y equals f of the modulus of x. Keep the right half where x is non-negative, and mirror it to the left, because the input's sign is erased, making the graph symmetric about the y-axis.
These are genuinely different operations that produce different graphs, and confusing them is a classic error.
The diagram sets them side by side: on the left the below-axis part flips up, on the right the right half is mirrored across the y-axis.
Here is the reference block: ranges first, then the identities that turn many problems into one-liners.
The ranges to lock in: modulus gives zero to infinity, signum gives the three values minus one, zero, one, floor gives the integers, and fractional part gives zero up to one.
For the growth pair, e to the x has range the strictly positive reals, while log base a has domain the strictly positive reals and range all the reals.
The modulus identities: the modulus squared equals x squared, the modulus of a product splits into a product of moduli, and signum times modulus rebuilds x itself.
The floor identities: x minus one is less than floor x, which is at most x, and shifting by an integer n moves the floor by exactly n.
A prized one for JEE: floor x plus floor of minus x is zero when x is an integer, and minus one otherwise. That off-by-one is a favourite trap.
The fractional part equals x minus floor x, with period one, and the log turns a product into a sum, the defining behaviour of logarithms.
Finally the change-of-base rule, log base a of x equals log base b of x over log base b of a, and a raised to log base a of x collapses back to x.

board_events.text: Read the values carefully
Now solve floor of x equals three; the answer is an interval, not a single point.
And fractional part equal to zero point five happens half-past every integer.
Floor equations give intervals: $[x]=3$ is all of $[3,4)$, never just $x=3$.
Split into cases, then intersect
For integer x, floor is x and fractional of minus x is zero, so f equals x.
For non-integer x the pieces fill each open gap, so the range is all reals.
A root in a denominator needs fractional part strictly positive, so exclude every integer.
Where standard functions slip
Floor of a negative rounds down: $[-2.3] = -3$, the single biggest source of lost marks.
$|f(x)|$ flips below-axis up; $f(|x|)$ mirrors the right half — never swap them.
Signum and floor output discrete values, not continuous bands.
Log needs its input above zero; the exponential output is always above zero, never touching it.
Speed pro-tips
For any floor or fractional problem, split into integer and non-integer cases immediately.
For fractional-part-equals-a-line, sketch the sawtooth against the line and count crossings.
Symmetry that halves your work
An even function has mirror symmetry about the y-axis; picture a parabola.
An odd function has rotational symmetry about the origin; picture x cubed or sine.
An odd function defined at $0$ passes through the origin: $f(0) = -f(0) \Rightarrow f(0) = 0$.
Most functions are neither; every function on a symmetric domain splits into an even plus an odd part.

segments.text: Let us evaluate the standard functions carefully, then solve two small equations that hide traps.

Floor of two point seven is two. Floor of minus two point three is minus three, rounding down past zero. And fractional part of three point six is three point six minus three, which is zero point six.
Signum of minus five is minus one, since only the sign survives, and the modulus of minus four is four.
Now solve floor of x equals three. This is not a single value; it asks which inputs floor to three.
The floor equals three for every x from three, inclusive, up to but not including four, so x lies in the interval three to four.
Next, fractional part of x equals zero point five. This holds whenever x is exactly half-past an integer.
So x equals n plus zero point five for any integer n, giving values like minus zero point five, zero point five, one point five, and so on.
Keep the trap in mind: a floor equation gives an interval, so floor of x equals three is all of three to four, never just x equal to three.
Two harder items now: a range that needs case-splitting, and a nested domain that combines several standard-function constraints.
Take f of x equals floor of x plus fractional part of minus x. The reliable move is to split into x integer and x non-integer.
For integer x, the floor is x and the fractional part of minus x is zero, so f of x is just x, an integer.
For non-integer x, the two pieces combine to give a value strictly between consecutive integers, so together with the integer case the range is all of the reals.
Now the nested domain: g of x equals one over the square root of the fractional part, plus log of one minus floor x, on the open interval minus three to three.
The first term has a root in the denominator, so it needs the fractional part strictly positive, which fails exactly at the integers. So exclude every integer.
The second term needs one minus floor x strictly positive, so floor x is at most zero, meaning x is less than one.
Combining on minus three to three: x below one with all integers removed leaves four open intervals, from minus three to minus two, and so on up to zero to one.
Let us close standard functions with the traps that leak marks, then the reflexes that crack these problems open.
Trap one, floor of a negative. Floor of minus two point three is minus three, not minus two. The floor always rounds down, and this is the single biggest source of lost marks here.
Trap two, mixing the modulus transforms. The modulus of f of x flips the below-axis part up, while f of the modulus of x mirrors the right half to the left. Never swap them.
Trap three, treating discrete ranges as intervals. Signum and floor output specific values or integers, not continuous bands.
Trap four, forgetting the growth domains. A log needs its input above zero, and the exponential output is always above zero, never actually equal to zero.
Now the reflexes that make these fast.
For any floor or fractional-part problem, split into x integer and x non-integer immediately. Almost every such problem cracks open that way.
And for a fractional-part-equals-a-line problem, sketch the sawtooth against the line and simply count the crossings.
Some functions carry a hidden symmetry that, once spotted, halves your work. There are two kinds to know.
An even function has mirror symmetry about the y-axis: whatever happens at x happens identically at minus x. Picture a butterfly, or the parabola y equals x squared.
Formally, even means f of minus x equals f of x. Fold the graph along the vertical axis and the two halves coincide exactly.
An odd function has rotational symmetry about the origin: flip it left-right and up-down and it lands on itself. Picture y equals x cubed, or y equals sine x.
Formally, odd means f of minus x equals minus f of x.
A neat consequence: if an odd function is defined at zero, it must pass through the origin, because f of zero equals minus f of zero forces f of zero to be zero.
Most functions are neither even nor odd, and that is fine. In fact, every function on a symmetric domain splits uniquely into an even piece plus an odd piece.
The diagram contrasts the two: the parabola mirrors across the vertical axis, while the cubic rotates onto itself about the origin.
The second form of redundancy is periodicity, the tendency of a function to repeat itself at fixed intervals.
A function is periodic if its graph repeats at regular intervals, like a heartbeat trace, the seasons, or a tabla rhythm cycling every few beats.
If the pattern repeats every T units, then f of x plus T equals f of x for all x, and the smallest such positive T is called the fundamental period.
Symmetry and periodicity are both forms of redundancy: the function tells you the same thing more than once, and exploiting that is where the speed comes from.
One caution. A constant function satisfies f of x plus T equals f of x for every T, so it is periodic but has no fundamental period, since there is no smallest T.
Another caution for sums. When you add two periodic functions, a common period exists only if their individual periods are commensurable, meaning their ratio is rational.
As a worked instance, the modulus of sine x plus the modulus of cosine x has fundamental period pi over two, because a shift by pi over two swaps the two moduli and leaves the sum unchanged.
The diagram marks one fundamental period T on a repeating wave: understand the function on that one stretch, and every other stretch is a copy.
Here is the rulebook: first how symmetry combines, then the standard periods and how they scale.
For sums and differences, even combined with even stays even, and odd combined with odd stays odd.
For products, even times even is even, odd times odd is even, and even times odd is odd. Watch that odd times odd flips to even, which surprises people.
The unique decomposition: the even part is f of x plus f of minus x, all over two, and the odd part is f of x minus f of minus x, all over two.
The standard periods to memorise: sine and cosine have period two pi, tangent and cotangent have period pi, the moduli of sine and cosine have period pi, and the fractional part has period one.
For an internal coefficient, f of a x plus b has period T over the absolute value of a, since the coefficient a compresses the cycle.
For a sum or difference, the period is the least common multiple of the two periods, but only when their ratio is rational.
And a handy pattern: taking an absolute value often halves the period, as the modulus of sine goes from two pi down to pi.

Take f of x equals x cubed minus x. Then f of minus x is minus x cubed plus x, which is minus f of x, so f is odd.
Take g of x equals x squared plus cosine x. Then g of minus x equals x squared plus cosine x, unchanged, so g is even.
Take h of x equals x plus x squared. Then h of minus x equals minus x plus x squared, which matches neither h of x nor minus h of x, so h is neither.
Now a speed question: pick the even one among sine x, x times the modulus of x, cosine x plus x squared, and x cubed.
Careful with x times the modulus of x. It looks even because of the modulus, but the lone x factor makes it odd, since odd times even is odd.
Scanning the rest, sine x is odd and x cubed is odd, so the only even function is cosine x plus x squared, an even plus an even.
And the fastest reflex of all: read polynomials off directly. Only even powers means even, only odd powers with no constant means odd.
Two examples here: finding a fundamental period of a sum, then splitting the exponential into its symmetric halves.

segments.text: Let us do a combination example, then a pattern-match on a functional equation.
Take f of x equals x squared and g of x equals two x plus one, both on the reals.
Their sum is x squared plus two x plus one, and their product is x squared times two x plus one, which expands to two x cubed plus x squared.
The quotient f over g is x squared over two x plus one, and its domain is all reals except minus one half, where the denominator vanishes.
Now a functional equation. A function satisfies f of x plus y equals f of x times f of y, with f of one equal to three. Find f of three.
This is the sum-to-product pattern, so f of x is a to the x. Since f of one is a, and that equals three, we have f of x equals three to the x.
Therefore f of three is three cubed, which is twenty seven. You can also get it directly, since f of three is f of one plus one plus one, equal to f of one cubed.
Watch the trap: treating this like the additive Cauchy equation would give three times f of one, that is nine. That is wrong, because the right side is a product, not a sum.
This example shows the substitute-and-eliminate technique, then sketches why the Cauchy equation gives a straight line.
Start with two f of x plus f of one minus x equals x squared. Call this equation one.
The unknown appears as both f of x and f of one minus x, so we need a partner equation. Replace x by one minus x.
That gives two f of one minus x plus f of x equals one minus x squared, which is equation two.
Now eliminate. Multiply equation one by two and subtract equation two, and the f of one minus x terms cancel, leaving three f of x equals two x squared minus one minus x squared.
Simplifying the right side gives x squared plus two x minus one, so f of x equals x squared plus two x minus one, all over three.
Finally, why does the Cauchy equation give a line? Setting x and y to zero forces f of zero to be zero, and letting k be f of one anchors the slope.
Additivity then transfers integer and rational scaling directly onto the function, and assuming continuity extends it to all reals, giving f of x equals k x.
Here is the reciprocal version of the elimination trick, finished with a verification you should always do.
Start with f of x plus two f of one over x equals three x. Call this equation one.
Since one over x appears inside f, replace x by one over x to build the partner equation.
That gives f of one over x plus two f of x equals three over x, which is equation two.
Now eliminate f of one over x. Multiply equation two by two, giving two f of one over x plus four f of x equals six over x, then subtract equation one.
The f of one over x terms cancel, leaving three f of x equals six over x minus three x, so f of x equals two over x minus x.
Always verify. Substitute back into the original: f of x plus two f of one over x becomes two over x minus x, plus two times two x minus one over x, which collapses cleanly to three x.
And keep the pattern in mind: the partner substitution is almost always x to one over x when one over x appears, or x to one minus x when one minus x appears.
Let us close the chapter's final subtopic with the traps, then the reflexes.
Trap one, dropping the domain in a combination. The quotient f over g excludes the zeros of g and respects both original domains, so intersect first, then delete the zeros.

Trap two, matching the wrong functional-equation pattern. Sum-to-sum is linear, sum-to-product is exponential, product-to-sum is logarithmic, and product-to-product is a power. Read the structure before solving.
Trap three, forgetting the second substitution. One equation relating f of x and f of something is not enough; you need a partner equation, generated by substituting a transformed x.
Trap four, assuming uniqueness without continuity. State the regularity assumption, and take the standard continuous solution that the substitutions produce.
Now the reflexes that make these quick.
Memorise the five standard patterns and their solutions, because then many find-f questions are recognised instantly with no work at all.
And always verify the final f by plugging it back into the original equation. It catches sign slips every single time.
Here is your complete Relations and Functions toolkit, gathered onto one board. This is a restatement for fast revision, not new teaching.

For relations, the four counts: two to the n squared relations overall, two to the n squared minus n reflexive, two to the n times n plus one over two symmetric, and the n-th Bell number for equivalence.
For functions, the four counts: m to the n functions, m permute n one-one, n factorial bijective, and the inclusion-exclusion alternating sum for onto.
For composition and inverse: the composite is g of f of x, the inverse of a composite reverses the order to f inverse ring g inverse, and a function is invertible exactly when it is bijective.
For domain and range: the three jams are denominator non-zero, even root non-negative, and log strictly positive, and the range of a linear-over-linear rational is all reals except a over c.

For the standard functions: modulus gives zero to infinity, fractional part lies in zero to one, the exponential is strictly positive, floor x plus floor of minus x is minus one off the integers, and signum times modulus rebuilds x.
For symmetry: the even and odd parts are the half-sum and half-difference of f of x and f of minus x, and f of a x plus b has period T over the absolute value of a.
And for functional equations: sum-to-sum gives k x, product-to-product gives x to the n, with the exponential and logarithmic patterns in between.

segments.text: This example drives home the single most common speed-trap error, declaring onto without checking the codomain.
Take f of x equals x squared plus one, and classify it in two cases that share the same formula but differ in codomain.
First the one-one verdict, which is the same for both cases. An even power means f of minus a equals f of a, so two inputs share one output, no algebra needed.
Concretely, f of two and f of minus two both equal five. Two inputs, one output, so the function is many-one in both cases.
Now case a, from the reals to the reals. The outputs satisfy x squared plus one is at least one, so the range is one to infinity.
That range is a strict subset of the reals, since everything below one is never hit, so case a is many-one and into.
Case b changes only the codomain, from the reals to the interval one to infinity. Now the range exactly equals the codomain.
So case b is many-one but onto. The one-one verdict never changed, yet flipping the codomain flipped the onto verdict. Never declare onto without checking B.
